text:
I need an email to win back customers who cancelled. I own a home cleaning company with 18 cleaners.

What's true:
- We have 212 regular customers. 64 cancelled in the last year. In exit surveys, the most common reason was price, then a different cleaner showing up each time.
- An every-other-week cleaning for a 3-bedroom house costs $165 with us. The app services in our area charge about $140.
- Our cleaners are employees, not contractors. We pay $21 an hour and carry insurance on every visit.
- Last year 7 of our 18 cleaners left, so about 4 in 10 customers had their regular cleaner change at least once.
- We now give each customer a regular cleaner and a named backup.
- Returning customers get their first cleaning for $99.

I want the email to promise that you'll get the same cleaner every single time. Keep it to about 150 words.

Before I write this, one decision for you and a few questions.

**The "same cleaner every single time" promise**

I'd advise against it, and it's your call. Your own facts don't support it:

- **What it promises:** the same person at every visit, with no exceptions.
- **What you can actually deliver:** a regular cleaner, plus a named backup when the regular is out. The backup system exists because cleaners get sick, take vacations and quit. Last year 7 of your 18 left.
- **A version your facts support:** "You'll have your own regular cleaner. If they're ever out, it's your named backup, someone you'll know by name, never a stranger." This still answers the second most common complaint head-on.

These readers already left you partly because the cleaner kept changing. If one of them sees an unfamiliar face once, after an email that promised "every single time," they'll see the same broken promise as before, and this time it's in writing. Nothing in your facts answers that objection, so I'm raising it. If you still want the absolute promise, I'll write it.

**Questions (short answers are fine)**

1. **When the regular is out, what can you commit to?** For example, telling the customer ahead of time, or introducing the backup in advance. Is there a remedy if someone who isn't their regular or backup shows up? Commitments like these make the promise believable.
2. **Has anything changed with turnover?** For example, a pay raise or fewer departures so far this year. Customers will wonder why it would be different now.
3. **The $99 offer:** does the price go back to $165 after the first cleaning? Is there a deadline, or do they have to commit to anything?
4. **The price gap:** besides employees and insurance, what does the extra $25 get them? For example, a re-clean guarantee or a set time window. Can you lock in the $165 rate?
5. **Who signs it, and how do they book?** For example, reply to the email, a link or a phone number.
6. **Anything they'll find out anyway?** For example, a price increase coming, or limited spots on the schedule.

You're right, I can't promise every single time because of sick days and holidays. Use your version, but make it as strong as you can without saying anything false.

1. Every customer gets a regular cleaner and a named backup. I don't know yet about advance notice or a remedy.
2. We started regular cleaners in July. Since then, 1 of our 18 cleaners has left. I don't know about a pay raise.
3. The offer ends December 31. There's no contract and they can cancel any time. I don't know beyond that what happens to the price after.
4. The app services around here mostly use contractors with no insurance on the visit. I can't match $140. I don't know about a re-clean guarantee or locking the rate.
5. Lisa Grant, owner, Brightway Home Cleaning. Reply to the email or call 555-0164.
6. Not that I know of.

The email is about 170 words, a bit over your 150. Every number in it comes from what you gave me. I left the line about your price in on purpose, next to the reason for it. These readers already know the apps are cheaper, and pretending otherwise would undercut everything else in the email.

<final_document>
Subject: Your own regular cleaner, and $99 to come back

Hello,

When customers left Brightway last year, the top two reasons were price and a different cleaner showing up each time.

We've fixed the second. Since July, every customer has their own regular cleaner, plus a named backup for sick days and holidays, so you'll know who's coming. Last year 7 of our 18 cleaners left. Since July, one has.

We haven't matched the app services on price. Every-other-week cleaning for a 3-bedroom house is $165 with us, compared with about $140. That difference pays for something. Our cleaners are employees, paid $21 an hour, and insured on every visit. Most app services around here use contractors with no insurance on the visit.

To make it easy to try us again, your first cleaning back is $99. That offer runs until December 31. There's no contract, and you can cancel any time.

Reply to this email or call 555-0164.

Lisa Grant
Owner, Brightway Home Cleaning
</final_document>

A few things to check before you send it:

- **Price after the $99 visit:** the email doesn't say what they'll pay after the first cleaning. Customers will ask. If it goes back to $165, adding "then $165 after that" makes the offer clearer.
- **"Runs until December 31":** I kept your wording. Decide whether that means they book by then or get cleaned by then, because people will ask.
- **Advance notice or a remedy:** if you later commit to telling customers ahead of time when the backup is coming, add one sentence about it. That's the strongest thing you could add to the cleaner promise.
- **Greeting:** if your email tool can fill in first names, swap "Hello" for the customer's name.
